lesson.title: Reassembling Text: The join() Method
lesson.summary: The join() method glues a list of strings back into a single string with a chosen separator, acting as the natural inverse of split().
lesson.body:
If split() breaks a string into a list of pieces, join() does the exact opposite: it takes a list (or any iterable) of strings and glues them back together into a single string, with a separator of your choosing placed between each piece. The syntax looks backwards the first time you see it, because the separator is the string the method is called on, not the list: separator.join(list_of_strings), not list_of_strings.join(separator). Keeping that order straight is the single biggest hurdle to using join() correctly.

Trace through an example. Suppose words = ["the", "quick", "brown", "fox"], the exact list you would get from splitting the sentence in the previous chapter. Calling " ".join(words) uses a single space as the separator: Python places "the", then a space, then "quick", then a space, then "brown", then a space, then "fox", producing the string "the quick brown fox" again. This is a genuine round trip: " ".join(sentence.split()) reconstructs the original sentence (assuming it only had single spaces to begin with), a good way to convince yourself that split and join are inverses of each other.

The separator does not have to be a space. "-".join(["2026", "08", "29"]) produces "2026-08-29", and ", ".join(["apples", "bread", "milk"]) produces "apples, bread, milk", a nicely formatted shopping list from a plain list of ingredients. An easy mistake is calling .join() on a list that contains something other than strings. "-".join([1, 2, 3]) raises a TypeError, because join() requires every element to already be a string. If you have a list of numbers, you must convert each one first, commonly with a list comprehension: "-".join([str(n) for n in [1, 2, 3]]) produces "1-2-3".

A practical use case is building a formatted line of output from data you collected piece by piece:

scores = [92, 85, 78, 100]
line = ", ".join(str(s) for s in scores)
print("Scores: " + line)

Here str(s) for s in scores is a generator expression that converts each integer to a string on the fly, and join() accepts it directly without needing a full list built first. The output is "Scores: 92, 85, 78, 100", a clean, human-readable summary built entirely from string methods.

Why prefer join() over building a string manually with a loop and +=? Efficiency and clarity both. Repeatedly concatenating strings with += inside a loop creates a new string object at every step, which becomes slow for long lists, while join() is optimized internally to assemble the whole result in one pass. When you see yourself accumulating text piece by piece in a loop, that is usually a sign join() on a list would be the cleaner choice.

The separator can also be an empty string, which simply concatenates every element with nothing between them: "".join(["a", "b", "c"]) produces "abc". This turns out to be the standard way to build a string from a list of individual characters, the reverse of the string iteration you will see in a later chapter, and it is a good reminder that join() works on any iterable of strings, not just a list literal, including a generator expression or the result of another string method.
